sysd-q-045.title: Streaming media
sysd-q-045.text: You can start watching a film before the file has finished arriving. That is streaming media. It is multimedia delivered over a network as a stream of packets and rendered in real time or near real time. A download is different: the user obtains the entire file first. Streams are compressed with video coding formats such as {{ref:sysd-q-105}} and {{ref:sysd-q-106}}, and assembled into a container such as MP4 or WebM. A streaming server delivers them by a transport protocol such as RTMP or RTP. In the 2010s, {{ref:sysd-q-043}}, Smooth Streaming, HDS and the non-proprietary {{ref:sysd-q-044}} emerged to give adaptive streaming over HTTP, as an alternative to proprietary transport protocols. A broadband speed of 2 Mbit/s or more is recommended for standard-definition video, 5 Mbit/s for high-definition and 25 Mbit/s for ultra-high-definition. UDP sends the stream as small packets, which is simple and efficient but gives no delivery guarantee. TCP guarantees delivery but stalls the stream on loss, which client buffering softens. Buffering delay is acceptable for {{ref:sysd-q-104}}, but video conferencing loses fidelity if it exceeds 200 ms.

sysd-q-047.title: Recommender system
sysd-q-047.text: Netflix tracks how you scroll, not only what you watch. Its engine records profile information, browsing and scrolling behavior, the time and date of viewing, the device used, and the number of searches and search terms. Those records feed a machine learning model built on viewing history. That is a recommender system: an information filtering system that suggests the items most relevant to a particular user, such as what to watch next. It matters wherever users face many options. {{ref:sysd-q-101}} builds a model from a user's past behavior and similar decisions by other users. Content-based filtering uses pre-tagged characteristics of items to recommend others with similar properties. The first needs a lot of data about a user, which is the cold start problem. The second needs very little to start but recommends only items similar to the seed. Most systems are hybrids that combine approaches, which can be more accurate and ease cold start and sparsity. Netflix uses a hybrid of similar users' habits and titles resembling those a user rated highly.

sysd-q-101.title: Collaborative filtering
sysd-q-101.text: The whole idea of collaborative filtering fits in one assumption: people who agreed before will agree again. It predicts a user's interests from taste information collected from many users. The assumption is that two people who share opinions on one issue are likelier to agree on others than a random pairing. The prediction is specific to the user but uses information from many users, unlike giving every item one average score. User-based filtering finds users with rating patterns like the active user's and predicts from their ratings. Item-based filtering, 'users who bought x also bought y', builds an item-item matrix and matches the user's data against it. Instead of explicit ratings it can use implicit observations, such as what a user listened to or bought. Its key challenges are cold start, where new users or items lack data, sparsity of the huge user-item matrix, and scalability. Open rating systems invite shilling attacks, with positive ratings for one's own items and negative ones for competitors'. And because it recommends from past ratings, it favors popular products.

sysd-q-102.title: Video codec
sysd-q-102.text: Raw video needs too much storage and bandwidth to record, send or stream. A codec fixes that. It is software or hardware that compresses and decompresses digital video, an encoder and a decoder in one, usually following a standard video coding format. Compression is typically lossy, so decompressed video has lower quality than the original. The bit rate trades off against quality, algorithm complexity, sensitivity to errors, random access and latency. Encoding usually subsamples the less perceptually important color information, applies a transform (the 8x8 DCT is most popular), quantizes the output and entropy-encodes the values. Decoding inverts each stage as far as possible, but quantization cannot be inverted, so decoding only approximates. Standards specify only the decoding process, so video quality can vary dramatically between encoders that use the same standard. As of 2016 the most widely used format was {{ref:sysd-q-105}}, with {{ref:sysd-q-106}} as its successor and the open, free VP8, VP9 and AV1 as alternatives.

sysd-q-042.title: Adaptive bitrate streaming
sysd-q-042.text: One video has to play well on a high-end connection and on a low-end one. Adaptive bitrate streaming does that: it encodes video at several bit rates and lets the player switch between them as bandwidth, CPU and device conditions change. An encoder encodes one source at multiple bit rates, and each stream is segmented into small multi-second parts. The client first downloads a manifest describing the segments and their bit rates. It starts with the lowest bit rate stream, requests a higher one when throughput exceeds the downloaded segment's bit rate, and a lower one when throughput deteriorates. The client's ABR algorithm decides which segments to download. Throughput-based algorithms use recent download throughput, buffer-based ones use only the buffer level, and hybrid ones combine both. Because it is built on HTTP, packets traverse firewalls and NAT, the server keeps no per-client session state, and existing HTTP caches and servers can be used. Delivered through content delivery networks, it scales to millions of concurrent viewers. The costs are extra encoding and storage, more complex operation than traditional streaming, and no single standard for digital rights management.

sysd-q-043.title: HTTP Live Streaming
sysd-q-043.text: In HTTP Live Streaming nobody downloads 'the video'. The player downloads a playlist, then the small segments it lists. HLS is an HTTP-based protocol from Apple for transferring unbounded streams of multimedia data, live or on demand. Version 7 is specified in RFC 8216. The receiver can adapt the bit rate to current network conditions to keep playback uninterrupted. A Media Playlist lists the Media Segments to play in sequence. A Master Playlist lists Variant Streams, each the same content at a particular bit rate, format and resolution. A segmenter, also called a packager, cuts the media into segments no longer than a constant target duration, typically 10 seconds, each with its own URI. Each segment has a unique Media Sequence Number, so clients can order and locate them. A live playlist is only appended to or trimmed from the front, and the server adds EXT-X-ENDLIST when the final segment is published. Because it is plain HTTP, it works with large-scale HTTP caching infrastructure, and segments can be encrypted.

sysd-q-104.title: Video on demand
sysd-q-104.text: Video on demand lets the viewer choose what to watch and when. It is a media distribution system that lets users access television shows, films and videos digitally on request. A selected video can begin playing immediately, which is streaming, or be downloaded for deferred viewing. Streaming has become the more popular way. The business models are subscription (SVOD, a regular fee for unlimited programs), transactional (TVOD, a fee per title) and advertising-based (AVOD, free to viewers). Near video on demand broadcasts copies of a programme at staggered intervals, typically every 10-20 minutes, which is bandwidth-intensive.

sysd-q-044.title: MPEG-DASH
sysd-q-044.text: Netflix and YouTube both support MPEG-DASH. It is Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP, an international-standard adaptive bitrate technique that streams media from conventional HTTP web servers. Content is split into small segments, each a short slice of playback time, and offered at several bit rates as alternative segments covering aligned intervals. During playback the client's adaptation algorithm picks the highest-bit-rate segment that can be downloaded in time to avoid stalls. The standard does not specify that logic. The reference client dash.js offers buffer-based (BOLA) and hybrid (DYNAMIC) algorithms. A media presentation description (MPD) describes each segment's timing, URL and media characteristics such as resolution and bit rate. DASH reuses existing HTTP web server infrastructure and is codec-agnostic. It is not a transport protocol. It was published as ISO/IEC 23009-1:2012 in April 2012. It is not directly supported in HTML5, so JavaScript players use the Media Source Extensions. Of the HTTP-based adaptive implementations, only DASH and HLS are still actively developed and used in 2026.

sysd-q-037.title: Video transcoding
sysd-q-037.text: A raw video is rarely the version a phone should receive. Video transcoding converts a video by decoding it to an intermediate uncompressed format, YUV for video, and re-encoding it into a target format and quality for different devices. It is needed when a target device does not support the format or has limited storage. The diversity of mobile devices makes it a must for mobile content adaptation. Raw video is transcoded into different compression rates and resolutions, such as mobile (720p), laptop (1080p) or high-resolution TV (4k), so the requested quality can be fetched. Transrating lowers the bitrate without changing the video format. Transsizing changes the picture size. The cost is quality. Transcoding to a lossy format loses detail, and the artifacts are cumulative, a loss called digital generation loss. So treat the original recording as the master copy and transcode each version only from it. Standalone tools such as FFmpeg or cloud services such as AWS Elemental MediaConvert can implement the step in a video pipeline.

sysd-q-036.title: Live streaming
sysd-q-036.text: A live stream has only a few seconds to get from camera to screen. Live streaming delivers video over the internet in real time, usually with a latency of just a few seconds. The camera and microphone capture raw video. It goes to the server side to be compressed and encoded to a standard such as {{ref:sysd-q-105}}, making the data much smaller. The encoded data is divided into segments, usually seconds long, so it takes much less time to download or stream. The streaming server must support different devices and network conditions, so it produces multiple files at different bitrates and uses adaptive bitrate streaming. Live data is pushed to CDN edge servers, so millions of viewers can watch from a nearby edge server, which significantly lowers transmission latency. Viewers' devices decode and decompress the data and play it. For replay, the encoded data also goes to a storage server that viewers can request from later. The standard protocols are {{ref:sysd-q-103}}, HLS and DASH, and HLS and DASH both support adaptive bitrate streaming. Video conferencing applications such as Skype use real-time communication protocols for lower latency.

sysd-q-046.title: Streaming delivery methods
sysd-q-046.text: If 1,000 people watch the same 300 kbit/s stream by unicast, the server needs 300 Mbit/s. With multicast it needs only 300 kbit/s. Unicast sends a separate copy to each recipient. It is the norm on the Internet but does not scale when many users want the same program. Multicast sends one stream to a group, cutting server and network load. It may not work on every network, and it loses video on demand functionality. Peer-to-peer protocols send prerecorded streams between computers so the server is not a bottleneck, but they raise technical, performance, security, quality and business issues. CDNs use intermediate servers to distribute the load.

sysd-q-103.title: Real-Time Messaging Protocol
sysd-q-103.text: RTMP keeps one TCP connection open and sends audio, video and control messages through it, interleaved. The Real-Time Messaging Protocol was built by Macromedia for Flash Player to stream audio, video and data over the Internet. It uses port 1935 by default, with persistent connections for low latency. After a handshake of three packets from each side, streams are split into fragments of dynamically negotiated size, by default 64 bytes for audio and 128 for video. Variants include RTMPS (over TLS), RTMPE (Adobe's encryption), RTMPT (tunneled in HTTP to pass firewalls) and RTMFP (over UDP). Enhanced RTMP widens its limited codec choice while staying compatible with existing infrastructure.

sysd-q-105.title: H.264
sysd-q-105.text: By December 2024, 79% of video industry developers used H.264, including streaming services such as Netflix, YouTube and Vimeo. Advanced Video Coding (AVC, H.264, MPEG-4 Part 10) is a block-oriented, motion-compensated video compression standard. It is by far the most commonly used video format. Savings of 50% or more in bit rate over MPEG-2 Part 2 are reported. The same digital satellite TV quality takes 1.5 Mbit/s with H.264 against around 3.5 Mbit/s with MPEG-2. High Profile is by far the most used of its profiles, the sets of capabilities for classes of applications. The format is patent-restricted, so commercial use requires royalties.

sysd-q-106.title: HEVC
sysd-q-106.text: HEVC compresses 25% to 50% better than {{ref:sysd-q-105}} at the same quality. High Efficiency Video Coding, or H.265, is a patent-encumbered standard published in 2013 as H.264's successor. For 4K at 30 frames per second it needs about 50 Mbps and 22.5 GB per hour, against 100 Mbps and 45 GB for older H.264 profiles. It uses coding tree units up to 64x64 samples instead of 16x16 macroblocks, which needs much more signal processing to compress. Licensing is the catch: combined patent fees are higher than for H.264, a main reason adoption on the web has been low.

sysd-q-107.title: AV1
sysd-q-107.text: In a 2020 study, AV1 encodes at 2160p took on average 590 times longer than AVC. AV1, AOMedia Video 1, is an open, royalty-free video coding format from the Alliance for Open Media, and the successor to VP9. Unlike {{ref:sysd-q-105}} and H.265, it is royalty-free, and its alliance was motivated by the high cost and uncertainty of {{ref:sysd-q-106}} patent licensing. The payoff is bandwidth: Netflix's 2017 tests found AV1 about 25% more efficient than VP9. The cost is compute. In the study VP9 took 5.2 times and HEVC 4.2 times as long as AVC. And 2017 decoding ran at about half the speed of VP9.

sysd-q-038.title: Geo-blocking
sysd-q-038.text: A film available in one country may be missing in the next. Geo-blocking is technology that restricts access to Internet content based on the user's geographical location. The location comes mainly from the IP address, mapped to a country or region with GeoIP databases. Netflix restricts content by region mainly because of legal distribution laws tied to deals with producers and distributors, while on YouTube the publisher chooses. Blocking can be network-level, filtering IP packets, or application-level, denying access after detecting the location. It is imperfect: IP-to-location mapping is inaccurate, and VPN or proxy services let users evade IP-based blocks.

sysd-q-035.title: Designing a video streaming service like Netflix
sysd-q-035.text:
A video streaming service like Netflix lets users stream and share videos, search by title or tag and comment, while a content team uploads new videos. It needs high availability with minimal latency, high reliability so no upload is lost, and scalability. The extended requirements are geo-blocking of certain content, resuming playback from where the user left off, and recording video metrics and analytics. The estimate is read-heavy: 1 billion total users, 200 million daily active users and 5 videos watched a day. That is 1 billion videos a day, 5 million uploads a day at a 200:1 read/write ratio, and 12K requests per second. At 100 MB per video, about 500 TB of storage is needed every day, and about 1,825 PB over 10 years. The minimum ingress bandwidth is around 5.8 GB per second.

The tables hold users, videos (title, streamURL, tags, userID), tags, views and comments. Each service owns its tables, on PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store such as Cassandra. Upload takes a title, description, byte stream and optional tags. Stream takes a video ID, codec, resolution and an optional offset in seconds. Search takes a query and an optional next-page token, and add comment takes a video ID and text. The system is built from microservices that each own their data model: user, stream, search, media for uploads and processing, and analytics. They communicate over REST or the lighter gRPC, with service discovery.

The hard part is upload. Two-hour raw 8K footage can reach 4 TB, so uploads go into a message queue such as Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ. Processing is a long-running task, and the queue decouples it from uploading. A file chunker splits each video by scene, not by equal timestamps, so a requested chunk is less likely to be interrupted. A machine-learning content filter checks for copyright, piracy and NSFW material and sends problems to a dead-letter queue. Then {{ref:sysd-q-037}} takes over. A transcoder decodes to an intermediate format and re-encodes with different codecs, using FFmpeg or AWS Elemental MediaConvert. The quality conversion yields 4K, 1440p, 1080p and 720p, stored in HDFS, GlusterFS or an object store such as Amazon S3.

Delivery is the other half. A CDN stops users from re-fetching the same content. Netflix's Open Connect partners with thousands of ISPs. It delivers around 95% of traffic over direct ISP connections from appliances in over 1000 locations, and fails over to Netflix servers. Adaptive bitrate protocols such as HLS adapt playback to network conditions, as {{ref:sysd-q-042}} explains. To resume playback, the offset stored in the views table retrieves the scene chunk at that timestamp.

Search runs on Elasticsearch. Trending content comes from caching the most frequently searched queries of the last N seconds and refreshing them every M seconds with a batch job. Geo-blocking, driven by legal distribution rights, finds the user's location by IP or profile region and redirects blocked users to an error page. A machine-learning model predicts what to watch next from viewing history. Cache static media with Redis or Memcached using LRU eviction, falling back to the database on a miss. Shard horizontally, using consistent hashing against uneven distribution.

To remove single points of failure, run multiple instances of each service. Place load balancers between clients, servers, databases and cache servers, and use read replicas and a replicated distributed cache. The thing to remember: most of the work happens before anyone presses play, in the queue, the chunker, the transcoder and the CDN.

sysd-q-041.title: Netflix's technology stack
sysd-q-041.text: Netflix's stack names a tool for each job, from the phone to the data warehouse. The native mobile apps are built in Swift and Kotlin and the web application in React, and GraphQL carries communication between the frontend and the server. Backend services rely on ZUUL, Eureka, the Spring Boot framework and other technologies. For data, the databases include EVCache, Cassandra and CockroachDB, and video is stored on S3 and served through Open Connect. Kafka and Flink handle messaging and streaming. Flink and Spark process data, which is visualized with Tableau, and Redshift holds structured data warehouse information. Delivering the software itself relies on CI/CD, the automated build and release pipeline, with tools such as Jenkins, Gradle, Spinnaker and Chaos Monkey.

sysd-q-039.title: YouTube's video transcoding unit
sysd-q-039.text:
YouTube handles 500+ hours of uploaded video every minute on average. Every upload must be transcoded: raw video is converted into different compression rates for different viewing devices, such as mobile (720p), laptop (1080p) or high-resolution TV (4k). Software-based encoding became slow and costly, so YouTube built a dedicated chip. It is the VCU, the Video transCoding Unit, developed for warehouse-scale video processing in the way GPUs and TPUs serve graphics and machine learning. The design is clusters of VCU servers, with accelerator trays of cards that hold encoders and decoders.

The VCU cluster generates the different resolutions and stores them in cloud storage. The design gave 20-33x improvements in computing efficiency over the previous optimized system. Transcoding, the step this unit serves, is described in {{ref:sysd-q-037}}.

sysd-q-040.title: Netflix Open Connect
sysd-q-040.text: Around 95% of Netflix's traffic globally is delivered over direct connections between Open Connect and the internet service providers (ISPs) that customers use to reach the internet. Open Connect is Netflix's purpose-built CDN, responsible for serving its video traffic, and it goes a step further than a traditional CDN. It places appliances at partner ISPs. Netflix partners with thousands of ISPs to localize its traffic and deliver content more efficiently. These Open Connect Appliances (OCAs) sit in over 1000 separate locations around the world. If an appliance has issues, it can fail over, and traffic is re-routed to Netflix servers. That makes it a private CDN: one company's own network, built to serve its own video traffic. For the general idea of a CDN and its edge servers, see {{ref:sysd-blocks-069}} and {{ref:sysd-blocks-070}}.

openers.design-a-video-streaming-service-like-ne: A video service sends a stream of packets that plays as it arrives, to viewers on very different devices and connections. This chapter follows a video from upload to screen. It starts with streaming itself and the codecs that compress video, then covers transcoding, adaptive bitrate streaming and its two main protocols, HTTP Live Streaming and MPEG-DASH. It also looks at the ways a stream reaches many viewers, from unicast copies to CDN servers, and adds recommendations and geo-blocking. It closes with a worked Netflix design and three case studies: Netflix's technology stack, YouTube's dedicated transcoding chip and Netflix Open Connect.

reviews.design-a-video-streaming-service-like-ne: Every video a viewer plays has passed through a chain this chapter followed link by link. Codecs such as H.264, HEVC and AV1 compress it, transcoding makes a version for each device, and adaptive bitrate streaming, as HLS or MPEG-DASH, lets the player move between those versions as bandwidth changes. A CDN then carries the segments close to viewers, which is why Netflix's Open Connect delivers around 95% of its traffic over direct ISP connections from appliances in over 1000 locations. Recommendation and geo-blocking sit on top, deciding what each viewer is offered and where. YouTube's VCU shows what happens when transcoding at scale, 500+ hours of uploads every minute, outgrows software.
